package bid

// roundToIntegral64 rounds the decimal x to an integral value in mode. The
// result exponent is max(Q(x), 0) whether or not a fraction was discarded
// (see "Exponent of a result"), which is exactly what round64 produces with
// floor 0: for Q(x) < 0 the value has fewer than Precision64 integer digits,
// so the least exponent at which the coefficient fits is the floor, and the
// digits below it are dropped and rounded; for Q(x) >= 0 nothing is
// dropped and the exact value is re-encoded at its own exponent, which also
// canonicalizes a non-canonical finite encoding. A zero keeps its sign and
// takes exponent max(Q(x), 0). A NaN gives that NaN made quiet and an
// infinity is returned unchanged.
func roundToIntegral64(x coef64, mode Mode) coef64 {
	kind, neg, c, exp := Unpack64(x)
	switch kind {
	case KindNaN:
		return cQuiet64(x)
	case KindInf:
		return cInf64(neg)
	}
	r, _ := round64(neg, wide64{Lo: c}, exp, classZero, mode, 0)
	return r
}

// quantize64 returns x with the exponent of y, rounded in mode, or the
// canonical NaN when the coefficient at that exponent has more than
// Precision64 digits. The exponent of y is in range, so a finite result
// never needs its exponent adjusted.
//
// When x has the larger exponent its coefficient is scaled up by the
// difference; round64 has nothing to round then (a coefficient padded to
// Precision64 digits or fewer at the exponent of y is already the result)
// but it is the one function that encodes a result. When x has the smaller
// exponent, round64 drops the digits below the exponent of y, with floor
// that exponent. Dropping at least one digit leaves at most Precision64-1
// digits, so rounding up cannot carry out of the coefficient, and
// an x so small that every digit is dropped rounds to zero or to one unit,
// whatever the distance. An exact zero takes the exponent of y.
func quantize64(x, y coef64, mode Mode) coef64 {
	xk, xneg, xc, xe := Unpack64(x)
	yk, ye := kindExp64(y)
	switch {
	case xk == KindNaN || yk == KindNaN:
		return nan64(x, y, y)
	case xk == KindInf && yk == KindInf:
		return cInf64(xneg)
	case xk == KindInf || yk == KindInf:
		return cNaN64()
	}
	if xe > ye {
		var overflow bool
		xc, overflow = cScale64(xc, xe-ye)
		if overflow || cGtMax64(xc) {
			return cNaN64()
		}
		xe = ye
	}
	r, _ := round64(xneg, wide64{Lo: xc}, xe, classZero, mode, ye)
	return r
}

// reduce64 returns the member of the cohort of x with the fewest coefficient
// digits: the trailing zeros of the coefficient are removed and the exponent
// raised to match, as far as MaxExp64 allows. A zero becomes a zero of its
// sign with exponent 0. A NaN gives that NaN made quiet and an infinity is
// returned unchanged.
func reduce64(x coef64) coef64 {
	kind, neg, c, exp := Unpack64(x)
	switch kind {
	case KindNaN:
		return cQuiet64(x)
	case KindInf:
		return cInf64(neg)
	}
	if cIsZero64(c) {
		exp = 0
	} else if q, r := cDivPow1064(c, 1); cIsZero64(r) && exp < MaxExp64 {
		// Strip the trailing zeros by binary search on their number, as key64
		// does, but never past MaxExp64. The number to strip, n, is at most
		// Precision64-1, below twice the first step, and each step takes a
		// power of two that n still contains: it can be removed exactly when
		// the coefficient divides by 10^step and the exponent has room.
		c, exp = q, exp+1
		step := 1
		for step*2 <= Precision64 {
			step *= 2
		}
		for ; step > 0; step /= 2 {
			if exp+step > MaxExp64 {
				continue
			}
			if q, r := cDivPow1064(c, step); cIsZero64(r) {
				c, exp = q, exp+step
			}
		}
	}
	r, _ := round64(neg, wide64{Lo: c}, exp, classZero, ToNearestEven, MinExp64)
	return r
}

// sameQuantum64 reports whether x and y are both finite with one exponent,
// both infinities or both NaNs.
func sameQuantum64(x, y coef64) bool {
	xk, xe := kindExp64(x)
	yk, ye := kindExp64(y)
	return xk == yk && (xk != KindFinite || xe == ye)
}

// quantum64 returns the quantum of x: for a finite x the positive value
// 1 × 10^Q(x), whose exponent is Q(x) and which is therefore always
// representable; for an infinity of either sign +∞; for a NaN that NaN made
// quiet. A non-canonical finite encoding reads as a zero with its encoded
// exponent, so its quantum is that of the zero.
func quantum64(x coef64) coef64 {
	kind, exp := kindExp64(x)
	switch kind {
	case KindNaN:
		return cQuiet64(x)
	case KindInf:
		return cInf64(false)
	}
	r, _ := round64(false, wide64{Lo: cPow1064(0)}, exp, classZero, ToNearestEven, MinExp64)
	return r
}
